summary: Norway is in the Schengen Area through the EEA: EU/EEA and Swiss citizens enter freely, around 60 visa-exempt nationalities including the US and UK get 90 days in any 180-day period counted across the whole Schengen Area, and everyone else needs a Schengen visa — while remote Svalbard is visa-free for all nationalities.

defaultStayWindow.text: 90 days in any rolling 180-day period, counted across the whole Schengen Area rather than per country. The day you arrive counts as the first day and the day you leave counts as the last. Leaving and coming back does not reset the allowance: on any given day, days already spent anywhere in the area during the preceding 180 still count against the 90.

source.name: European Commission — Schengen short-stay calculator (DG Migration and Home Affairs)

fee.notes: Children 6–11: €45; under 6: free. Fee set EU-wide since June 11, 2024; paid in local currency where you apply.

visaTypes.name: National Long-Stay Visa / Residence Permit (Type D)

fee.notes: Stays over 90 days (work, study, family) are handled as residence-permit applications through UDI; fees vary by purpose. Confirm the current fee on udi.no before applying.

passportValidity.text: Non-EU passports must be valid for at least 3 months beyond your planned departure from the Schengen Area and have been issued within the last 10 years. EU/EEA citizens only need a valid passport or national ID card.

travelInsurance.text: Schengen visa applicants must hold travel medical insurance covering at least €30,000, valid across the Schengen Area for the whole stay. Visa-exempt visitors are not required to show it, but medical care is expensive — cover is strongly recommended.

onwardTicket.text: Border officers may ask non-EU visitors for proof of return or onward travel and accommodation details.

proofOfFunds.text: A commonly used guideline is around NOK 500 per person per day. Visa-free visitors are rarely checked, but visa applicants must document their means. Confirm current expectations with UDI.

declarations.name: EES — Entry/Exit System (biometric registration)
declarations.submitWindow: At the border on first entry
declarations.text: Non-EU travelers are registered biometrically (fingerprints and photo) in the EU Entry/Exit System at Schengen external borders. Registration happens at the border. There is nothing to submit in advance, but allow extra time on your first entry.

declarations.name: ETIAS — European Travel Information and Authorization System

fee.notes: Free for under-18s and over-70s. Valid 3 years or until passport expiry.

declarations.text: Visa-exempt travelers will need an ETIAS travel authorization to enter the Schengen Area. It is being phased in. Check the official EU site for the current status and apply only there.

currencyLimits.text: Cash and other means of payment worth NOK 25,000 or more must be declared when entering or leaving Norway.

notes: Norway is not in the EU customs union — normal duty-free limits apply even when arriving from EU countries.
Alcohol and tobacco quotas are small and strictly enforced; declare anything above them at the red channel.

payments.text: Norway is close to cashless. Cards and mobile payments are accepted everywhere, including buses, kiosks and public toilets, and some places no longer take cash at all.

safety.text: Norway is one of the safest countries in the world, with very low crime. The main risks are outdoors: fast-changing mountain and sea weather, and winter road conditions.

source.name: UK Foreign, Commonwealth & Development Office — Norway travel advice

bestTimeToVisit.text: May–September brings long days, open mountain roads and the midnight sun in the north; for northern lights aim for September–March in Tromsø or Lofoten instead.

idp.text: Norway is a party to both the 1949 Geneva and the 1968 Vienna Conventions on Road Traffic, so it recognizes an International Driving Permit issued under either.

source.name: UN Treaty Collection — Convention on Road Traffic (Vienna, 1968), status of parties
source.instrument: Convention on Road Traffic, Geneva, 19 September 1949 (UNTS vol. 125, p. 3); Convention on Road Traffic, Vienna, 8 November 1968 (UNTS vol. 1042, p. 17)

driving.text: Norway is a party to both the 1949 Geneva and the 1968 Vienna Conventions on Road Traffic, so it recognizes an International Driving Permit issued under either. Whether a permit is required in addition to a national license, and for how long a foreign license may be used, are set by national road law and have not been checked for Norway yet.

source.name: UN Treaty Collection — Convention on Road Traffic (Vienna, 1968), status of parties
source.instrument: Convention on Road Traffic, Geneva, 19 September 1949 (UNTS vol. 125, p. 3); Convention on Road Traffic, Vienna, 8 November 1968 (UNTS vol. 1042, p. 17)

tips.text: Svalbard is outside the Schengen Area and visa-free for all nationalities, but the only practical route is via mainland Norway, so travelers who need a Schengen visa should request a double-entry visa to come back through Oslo or Tromsø.
Norway is one of Europe's most expensive countries and largely cashless. Budget generously for food and transport and don't bother changing much cash.
Wine and spirits are sold only in state Vinmonopolet shops with limited hours (closed Sundays), and supermarket beer sales stop early in the evening. Plan ahead.
Mountain and fjord weather changes fast even in summer. Check conditions before hikes like Trolltunga or Preikestolen and carry proper gear; rescues are frequent among unprepared visitors.

faq.question: Do I need a visa for Norway?
faq.answer: EU/EEA and Swiss citizens don't need a visa at all. Citizens of around 60 visa-waiver countries — including the US, UK, Canada, Australia and Japan — can visit visa-free for up to 90 days in any 180-day period, counted across the whole Schengen Area. All other nationalities need a Schengen short-stay visa applied for through the Norwegian mission or visa center serving their place of residence.

faq.question: Do I need a visa for Svalbard?
faq.answer: No — Svalbard is visa-free for all nationalities under the Svalbard Treaty. However, flights go via mainland Norway, which is in Schengen, so if you need a Schengen visa you must hold one that lets you transit Norway (ideally double-entry) to reach and leave Svalbard.

faq.question: Does time in Norway count toward the Schengen 90/180-day limit?
faq.answer: Yes. Norway is not in the EU, but it applies Schengen rules fully through the EEA — days spent in Norway are counted together with days in France, Germany and the rest of the Schengen Area.

faq.question: How long can UK citizens stay in Norway?
faq.answer: UK passport holders can visit visa-free for up to 90 days in any 180-day period, shared with the rest of the Schengen Area. The passport must have been issued within the last 10 years and be valid for at least 3 months beyond departure.

faq.question: Do I need ETIAS to visit Norway?
faq.answer: Once ETIAS becomes mandatory, visa-exempt travelers will need the authorization (€20, valid 3 years) for Norway as for the rest of the Schengen Area. It is being phased in. Check the official travel-europe.europa.eu site for the current status.
